correctness.rationale: The proof defines the geodetic interval as the union of all shortest paths. Its incidence analysis shows all covered point-vertices lie in selected points or on selected lines, and dually all lines pass through selected points or are selected. Sharp q-line/q-point union bounds force at least 2q vertices; simultaneous equality forces exactly q concurrent selected lines and the complementary q points, with unique flag parameter. Direct length-2 and length-3 geodesics show each constructed basis works. Pairwise overlap counts are derived by incidence case split and give three exact replacement distances and a connectedness threshold, including the special q=2 opposite-flag argument. Exhaustive independent shortest-path computations confirm all bases for q=2,3; an independent finite-field construction confirms witnesses and pairwise metrics for q=2,3,4,5. The universal proof does not rely on finite experiments.

originality.rationale: A statement-level comparison found no cited or surfaced theorem that determines the geodetic number, all flag-shaped minimum geodetic bases, their exact number and the first simultaneous-exchange connectivity threshold for every finite projective-plane incidence graph. Classical geodetic-set bounds and constructions apply to broader graph classes but do not supply these plane-specific equality cases. Records on complete multipartite and crown graphs concern nonisomorphic structural families and imply no such classification. The search cannot establish uniqueness; incomplete foundational full-text access and unindexed literature remain genuine residual risks.

value.rationale: The original problem is minimum shortest-path coverage of an incidence geometry. The theorem supplies a universal, exact minimum and all equality cases, including non-Desarguesian planes, and an exact, sharp reconfiguration barrier: no optimal one-vertex moves, but global mobility begins at precisely min(q+1,2q−2) simultaneous replacements. Flag geometry gives a structural explanation for both enumeration and reachability, which could not be inferred from a scalar bound or isolated numerical table. The result is neither an arbitrary finite slice nor a mere substitution into a textbook formula; the incidence geometry and optimal-solution space are mathematically natural.
